strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: measuring social biases in masked language models and tracking changes after continued pretraining. Its focus on masked-token prediction provides a clear operational setting.

The experiments cover four models, two established benchmarks, several existing measures, and detailed category-level results. These comparisons usefully demonstrate that bias estimates depend on both the benchmark and the scoring method.
Training on opposite members of stereotype pairs provides a useful initial sensitivity check. Explicit equations, token-level examples, and distribution plots help explain the proposed measures.
weaknesses: The human-annotation experiment does not establish the claimed superiority in measuring model bias. Its labels indicate whether sentence pairs express recognizable stereotypes, rather than the direction or magnitude of a model’s bias. Figure 3 also shows weak discrimination: the best proposed AUROC is 0.571 versus 0.569 for AUL on BERT, and 0.572 versus 0.560 on RoBERTa. With only 58 negative pairs and no confidence intervals or paired significance tests, these differences provide insufficient evidence of improvement. The description of selecting thresholds to maximize AUROC is also unclear.

The retraining evaluation does not separate memorization from transferable social bias. Section 4.3 trains on 80% of the CPS sentences, while the reported evaluation uses the full benchmark categories; no independent test evaluation is reported. The claimed 100% accuracy concerns 72 aggregate direction predictions whose labels are assumed from the training condition. This supports sensitivity to training exposure, but does not establish accurate measurement of social bias. Evaluation on unseen pairs and balanced or neutral training controls is needed.

The interpretation of score differences exceeds the available construct validation. Whole-sentence prediction quality can reflect lexical frequency, tokenization, and general predictability alongside stereotypical associations. The paper does not adequately isolate these effects. Consequently, statements that competing measures underestimate disability or religious bias are unsupported: disagreement with the proposed measures does not establish which estimate is correct.

The statistical analyses do not consistently support the stated conclusions. Welch’s independent-samples test ignores the matched sentence-pair design. Section 4.2 infers stronger race bias from significance within individual models without directly testing differences between models. McNemar’s test evaluates changes in binary preference signs, whereas Equation 16 counts increases in continuous score differences; its significance markers therefore do not directly test the displayed statistic. Uncertainty estimates and treatment of the many comparisons are also missing.

Reproducibility and baseline fidelity remain unresolved. Optimizer, learning rate, batch size, random seeds, and precise attention aggregation are unspecified. Equations 1–2 sum over all sentence tokens, although the accompanying descriptions define CSPS over unmodified tokens and SSS over modified tokens. These discrepancies must be resolved to reproduce the comparisons reliably.

The contribution of individual modifications is not isolated. CRR and the probability-gap approach build directly on prior work, while CRRA changes the rank transformation as well as adding attention weights. Ablations separating logarithmic transformations, attention weighting, and token-selection policy, including a standard all-token pseudo-log-likelihood baseline, would clarify what produces the reported differences. The decisive barriers to Findings are the validation and reproducibility gaps, rather than the incremental nature of the methods; addressing them warrants resubmission next cycle.
